title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: The diff module compares two byte slices and returns an edit script in line counts. Use line_diff(from, to, options, limits) when a caller needs Fossil’s line matching and edit ordering without a rendered patch. Bytes need not be valid UTF-8. The module opens no files or databases. title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: line_diff returns Result , DiffError>. Each Edit has three counts: Field Lines consumed copy Common lines from both inputs. delete Lines from FROM only. insert Lines from TO only. Read each triple in that order. Advance FROM by copy + delete and TO by copy + insert. The vector ends with the native zero triple, whose three counts are zero. Inserted content comes from TO. The script holds counts and omits line bytes. LF separates lines and is excluded from comparison. An unterminated final line still counts as a line. Adding or removing its final LF alone produces no line change. An empty input has zero lines.

title: Compare normalized byte lines
text: LineDiffOptions::default() selects exact comparison, native readability optimization and no other option. Choose these fields for each call: Field Behavior whitespace: Whitespace::Exact Compare all bytes within a line. whitespace: Whitespace::IgnoreEol Ignore trailing Fossil whitespace bytes. whitespace: Whitespace::IgnoreAll Ignore Fossil whitespace throughout a line. strip_cr Remove a trailing CR from each line before comparison. invert Exchange FROM and TO before computing edits. optimize Apply native readability shifts to insertions and deletions. not_too_big Reject more than 10,000 inserted plus deleted lines. Fossil whitespace here means bytes 8, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 32. It is not Unicode whitespace. IgnoreEol and IgnoreAll return the error DiffError::WhitespaceOnly when the script has one copy-only triple followed by the zero triple. They can also return scripts that contain edits.

Applications can choose smaller bounds for their inputs: Field Default and meaning max_input_bytes 16 MiB combined input bytes. max_lines 200,000 combined input lines. max_edits 200,001 triples, including the final zero triple. max_work 100,000,000 charged inspections, comparisons and search iterations. The implementation also caps combined bytes at i32::MAX and combined lines at 1,000,000, even when caller limits are larger. Work is a charged algorithm budget. It does not measure each processor instruction or total heap bytes. Input bounds are checked before line-table allocation, and reservations can fail. DiffError::Binary reports an embedded NUL or a line longer than 32,767 bytes. WhitespaceOnly reports the rejection described above for the whitespace modes. TooManyChanges reports the enabled change-count rejection. Limit reports a caller bound or fixed cap, checked arithmetic failure or allocation failure. A failure returns no partial script.

It requires the same provider patches shown above and fresh qualification of this adaptation. use gossil::glob::{glob_create, glob_expr, glob_multi_match, Limits}; let limits = Limits { list_bytes: 1024, candidate_bytes: 1024, patterns: 16, expression_bytes: 4096, }; let list = Some(b"*.rs,src/*".as_slice()); let patterns = glob_create(list, limits).unwrap(); assert_eq!(patterns.glob_match(b"src/lib.rs").unwrap(), 1); assert_eq!(glob_multi_match(list, b"notes.md", limits).unwrap(), 0); assert_eq!(glob_expr(b"?1", list, limits).unwrap(), b"(?1 GLOB '*.rs' OR ?1 GLOB 'src/*')"); Handle GlobError in an application. ?1 is a trusted parameter expression; bind the candidate separately when executing this SQL through your own database interface. glob_expr returns bytes and executes no SQL. title: Lexical file paths
text: The gossil::file_path module simplifies filename bytes by the rules of Fossil’s file_simplify_name function. Lexical simplification changes only the bytes of the name. It does not read the filesystem, resolve symlinks or make a name absolute. The native C source has one branch for Unix and one for Windows and Cygwin. The module ports both source branches, and the caller selects one of them on every host.

title: Lexical file paths
text: simplify_name(input, keep_trailing_slash, limits) uses the Unix branch and returns Result , PathError>. Give the complete filename as a byte slice, which does not have to be UTF-8. An empty input gives an empty output, and an input that contains a NUL byte is an error. use gossil::file_path::{Limits, simplify_name}; let limits = Limits { max_input_bytes: 128, max_output_bytes: 128 }; let path = simplify_name(b"a/b/../c/", false, limits).unwrap(); assert_eq!(path, b"a/c"); simplify_name_for_source(input, keep_trailing_slash, limits, platform) takes a SourcePlatform and returns Result . Source choice Behavior SourcePlatform::Unix Backslashes and extended prefixes stay ordinary bytes SourcePlatform::WindowsCygwin Backslashes become slashes, and the //?/ extended prefix is removed The source choice does not depend on the host operating system. A choice of WindowsCygwin does not show that Gossil runs correctly on Windows or Cygwin.

title: Lexical file paths
section: Read the result of a source branch
text: A SimplifiedName has two views of its bytes: reported_span() borrows the bytes that the native return value counts. visible_bytes() borrows the bytes before the first NUL, as a C string shows them. The two views differ for one input. For the Windows/Cygwin input //?/, native C copies the terminator of the input to byte zero but reports a length of one. So the reported span is [0], and the visible name is empty.

title: Lexical file paths
text: Limits has the fields max_input_bytes and max_output_bytes. The input must fit its limit. The module reserves one buffer of the input length plus one sentinel byte, the C terminator, before it copies the input. The output limit counts the reported span, and the span can hold an early NUL. So the input //?/ needs an output limit of at least one with WindowsCygwin, but its visible name is empty. Error Condition InputLimit The input exceeds its limit, or the buffer exceeds addressable memory OutputLimit The reported span exceeds its limit EmbeddedNul The input contains NUL TerminalCancellation A relative name cancels to before the start of the buffer Allocation The buffer reservation fails, and the error keeps the original cause

title: Lexical file paths
section: The order of the lexical rules
text: The module follows the loops of the native function in their order: With WindowsCygwin, it converts each backslash to a slash, then handles an initial //?/. If keep_trailing_slash is false, it trims the trailing slashes. It collapses duplicate slashes, but keeps an initial double slash. It removes leading ./, internal /./ and each /component/.. that can cancel. For example, //a stays //a, but // becomes / when keep_trailing_slash is false. Unresolved .. components stay, even above an absolute root. A nonempty name that simplifies to nothing becomes /. The trailing slash option does not keep every trailing slash. With the option true, a/// becomes a/, but a///./ becomes a. The second result comes from the collapse loop. The loop shortens the logical length but leaves the old bytes after it. A later /./ test can read those bytes, and the port keeps this behavior. With WindowsCygwin, the module compares the three bytes after //?/ with UNC, and it ignores ASCII case, as SQLite’s sqlite3_strnicmp does. A match gives an initial slash and skips UNC. So //?/UNC/a/b becomes //a/b. Without a match, the byte after the prefix moves to the start, and //?/a:/a/b becomes a:/a/b. The port does not check drives, the names after the UNC prefix or whether a name is valid.

title: Lexical file paths
section: When a relative name cancels past its start
text: A relative name such as a/.. cancels its last component back past the start of the name. The case is a relative terminal cancellation. Native backup_dir then leaves the output cursor at minus one, so native C writes the final terminator one byte before the buffer. The write is undefined behavior, and native Fossil has no defined result for these names. The port returns PathError::TerminalCancellation in place of a result. Examples are a/.., .../.. and a/../ with the trailing slash option false. The error is a safe policy of the port, and not a native result.

title: Gest author values
text: The gossil::gest_author_values module validates all six canonical author fields in memory. Use it for complete decoded snapshots before storage integration. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. An author record identifies a human or agent in its record model. Accepting the human value here does not deliver native Human workflows. AuthorValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for gest_id, author_type, name, email, created_at and updated_at. author_from_values returns an AuthorValues record with private fields. author_to_values returns all six fields as independent owned values. See library setup for Cargo dependencies.

title: Gest author values
text: Before decoding raw input, check required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Decoding can collapse duplicate keys. Then supply every field, including an explicit null for absent email. use gossil::gest_author_values::{AuthorValueInputs, author_from_values, author_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let author = author_from_values(AuthorValueInputs { gest_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), author_type: json!("AGENT"), name: json!(" Alice "), email: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-19T01:02:03.000000001+02:00"), updated_at: json!("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"), }).unwrap(); let values = author_to_values(&author); assert_eq!(values.author_type, json!("agent")); assert_eq!(values.name, json!(" Alice ")); assert_eq!(values.email, json!(null)); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T23:02:03.000000001+00:00")); assert_eq!(author_from_values(values).unwrap(), author); The modification time precedes creation in this example because conversion imposes no time ordering. It generates no identity or time and performs no SQL.

title: Gest author values
text: The identifier must contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. The author type accepts case-insensitive human or agent and emits lowercase. It rejects surrounding whitespace and other values. Names accept any string, including empty strings, whitespace and control characters. Email accepts an explicit null or any string. Null and an empty string remain distinct. Conversion does not check email syntax or trim either field. Both timestamps require strings that chrono 0.4.44 can parse as RFC3339. Conversion normalizes each instant to UTC and checks that its output can be parsed again. It rejects output outside that canonical RFC3339 domain. AuthorValueError displays the field and a static reason without echoing input. Its parse_cause() accessor returns the actual chrono error from input parsing or canonical output parsing. Other failures have no parser cause.

title: Gest author values
text: Callers own raw decoding, field admission, duplicate detection, byte limits, reference checks and the history of changes to the record. An author record is separate from native actor bytes and local principals. Conversion does not establish uniqueness, authorization, storage, lifecycle, replay, migration or the complete Gest API. The seven controls in tests/gest_author_values.rs cover field types, identifiers, author types, exact strings, nullable email, timestamps, parser causes and owned output. These controls exercise the pure converter. They do not test storage or native workflows. Their presence does not establish an executed test pass.

title: Gest project values
text: The gossil::gest_project_values module converts all four canonical project fields into an owned, validated record. Use it for complete decoded snapshots before storage integration. Project persistence and CLI commands remain planned. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. These converters use its task and project record model. A Gest project represents a tracked repository or directory. Here, canonical means the four project fields in the reviewed field map. In a source checkout, the map is tests/fixtures/gest_project_values/source-map.json. ProjectValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for gest_id, archived_at, created_at and updated_at. project_from_values returns a ProjectValues record with private fields. project_to_values returns all four fields as independent owned values. The local checkout root is a filesystem path and is not canonical data. The upstream project model defines the source record. See library setup for Cargo dependencies.

title: Gest project values
text: Before constructing serde_json::Value inputs, callers check raw JSON for required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Duplicate keys must be checked before decoding collapses them. Then assemble every field for conversion. Nullable archive state requires an explicit null. The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_project_values::{ProjectValueInputs, project_from_values, project_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = ProjectValueInputs { gest_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), archived_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"), }; let project = project_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = project_to_values(&project); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(project_from_values(values).unwrap(), project); The example sets modification before creation to show that conversion imposes no time ordering.

title: Gest project values

ProjectValueError displays the field and a static reason without echoing input. Its parse_cause() accessor retains the actual chrono error from input parsing or canonical UTC output parsing. Other failures have no parser cause. Callers own raw decoding, required-field presence, unknown-field classification, duplicate keys in the original input, byte budgets and reference checks. title: Gest task values
text: The gossil::gest_task_values module converts eleven already decoded task fields into an owned, validated record. Callers can use the record for complete task snapshots before storage integration. Pass validated snapshots to the task ticket emitter for bounded creation artifact bytes. The module does not implement the full Gest API or migrate stored repositories. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. This converter uses its task record model. Here, canonical values use the status and UTC timestamp forms defined below. TaskValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for each field. task_from_values validates these values and returns TaskValues, whose fields are private. task_to_values returns the complete set of owned values. The functions do not read a clock, generate identifiers or execute SQL.

title: Gest task values
text: Check raw input field presence, duplicates and byte limits before assembling decoded values. No field has a default. The public input and output use the same TaskValueInputs type. use gossil::gest_task_values::{TaskValueInputs, task_from_values, task_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = TaskValueInputs { gest_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), project_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), title: json!("Review task values"), priority: json!(255), status: json!("IN_PROGRESS"), description: json!(""), assigned_to: json!(null), metadata: json!([null, {"reviewed": false}]), resolved_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let task = task_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = task_to_values(&task); assert_eq!(values.status, json!("in-progress")); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(task_from_values(values).unwrap(), task); The example uses array metadata and priority 255 to show the model’s full value types. Production callers must handle TaskValueError from validation. Its display text names the first rejected field and the reason, without echoing the supplied value. TaskValueError::parse_cause() returns the original chrono::ParseError when parsing the input or its canonical UTC output fails. Callers can inspect its kind() to distinguish failures such as TooShort and OutOfRange. Other validation failures return no parse cause. Error equality includes the retained cause, so errors with equal display text can compare unequal. Chrono’s alloc-only build does not implement std::error::Error for this parser error, so callers use the accessor rather than Error::source(). The validated record stays unchanged if a caller changes the owned fields returned by task_to_values.

title: Gest task values
text: The input requires all eleven fields, even when a value is null. Field Admitted value gest_id Full task ID string, called id in Gest’s task Model. project_id Full project ID string. title Any string. priority Null or a JSON integer from 0 through 255. status A status string accepted by Gest’s task status FromStr implementation. description Any string. assigned_to Null or a full author ID string. metadata Any serde_json::Value, including null. resolved_at A timestamp string for terminal status, otherwise null. created_at A timestamp string. updated_at A timestamp string. The task and project identifiers require exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. An assignee is null or a full identifier. Title and description preserve their strings, including empty strings, Unicode, whitespace and null characters. The task field gest_id corresponds to upstream Model.id. Priority is null or an integer from 0 through 255. Checked conversion rejects negative integers, larger integers, floating point values and other JSON types. The upstream task model uses Option . Its separate named priority enum covers only 0 through 4 and is outside this module. Status parsing follows upstream FromStr. The statuses are open, in-progress, done and cancelled. Parsing accepts case differences and the in-progress, in_progress and inprogress aliases. Output uses in-progress. The adopted Gossil contract requires a resolution timestamp for done and cancelled, and null for open and in-progress. The converter checks that pairing without generating a timestamp. Metadata retains every JSON value variant, including null. Explicit metadata null is model data, independent of the nulls in optional model fields. The converter preserves JSON value semantics without promising original JSON spelling, object member order or duplicate-key detection. Business timestamps use Gest’s pinned chrono 0.4.44 RFC3339 parser and normalize to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), subject to Gossil’s canonical output contract. RFC3339 is the timestamp string format used at this boundary. Output uses chrono’s RFC3339 form with the +00:00 offset and at most nine fractional digits. The parser accepts offsets, lowercase separators, a space separator, year zero and leap seconds. It truncates fractional input beyond nanoseconds, as upstream does. Business timestamp rules are separate from the stricter artifact D-card time grammar. The converter adds no ordering rule between timestamps. A parsed instant must have a UTC representation that the RFC3339 parser can read back. Offset normalization across the year zero or 9999 boundary can produce a signed extended year. The converter rejects those results under the adopted output contract. Upstream source parsing accepts their inputs. Year zero and nearby offsets remain valid when their UTC result is representable. The module does not claim parity with the full upstream timestamp input domain. Invalid field types, incomplete identifiers, invalid priorities or statuses, unparseable timestamps and inconsistent status/resolution pairs return TaskValueError. Normalized UTC output outside the adopted RFC3339 domain also returns that error. Metadata has no further type restriction.

title: Get started
text: Use Gossil to create a delta between two files and restore the target exactly. A delta encodes target bytes as new bytes and copies from an origin file. This exercise needs no repository and does not change Git history. Gossil is intended to keep agent files, issues and their history alongside Git. Its command line initializes and opens repositories, tracks explicit files, selects their scopes, records private history and has three delta diagnostics. The Rust library also supports artifact parsing, local storage and task, project and author conversion. Try the delta commands below. Read working with repositories for the intended file and issue workflows.

title: Get started
text: Install Git, Rust with Cargo, Just, uv and the jlog command recorder. These tools must be available on PATH. Rust builds also need the native compiler and platform development tools used by Cargo dependencies. Linux setup also requires Make, zlib development headers and CA certificates to build the pinned Tcl and Fossil references. On other hosts, supply the reference prerequisites before setup. The commands below use a POSIX shell, such as the default shell on macOS or Linux. git clone https://github.com/rahuldave/gossil.git cd gossil just setup just setup supplies the Linux references or checks the existing tools on other hosts, then fetches the Cargo dependencies. just gossil then builds and runs the source executable through jlog and Cargo. You do not need a globally installed gossil executable. The first build can take longer than later calls. The example builds from source. Keep the checkout open in this shell for the following commands. The contributor setup is for people who also need the optional workflow packages and verification guidance.

title: Get started
text: Make a fresh scratch folder so that the example cannot overwrite earlier work. Keep the quotation marks around paths so that paths with spaces work too. example_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/gossil-example.XXXXXX) printf 'before\n' > "$example_dir/origin" printf 'after\n' > "$example_dir/target" just gossil vcs test-delta-create "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/change.delta" The arguments are the original file, the desired file, and the delta to write. Success writes change.delta and prints no command output. Cargo can print build messages on stderr. A delta need not be smaller than its target, especially for small files like these.

title: Get started
text: Apply the delta to the same origin, writing a separate restored file: just gossil vcs test-delta-apply "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/change.delta" "$example_dir/restored" cmp "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/restored" cat "$example_dir/restored" cmp prints nothing and exits with status 0 when the files match. cat prints after. The original and target files remain available. To check that Gossil can create and apply deltas in both directions, run: just gossil vcs test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" Success prints ok. This command checks the round trip in memory. It does not save another delta or create a check-in. You can repeat these commands with text or binary files. A delta describes bytes, so keep its matching origin when you need to restore the target later.

title: Get started
text: v is the short name for vcs: just gossil v test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" The source also builds a gos executable with the same diagnostics. See short executable names for its source invocation. The same aliases support native checkout open. Issue commands, shared recording and sync remain planned.

title: Get started
section: Handle failures and choose the next step
text: A diagnostic exits with status 1 and writes an error to stderr when it fails. Check the input paths and argument order first. If applying a delta fails, check that you kept the correct origin and an intact delta. The CLI reference lists the exact messages. Successful create and apply operations replace an existing output file. Use a fresh output path until you have checked the result. Validation failures preserve the output, but a write failure can leave it truncated. The repository guide explains how a file delta differs from a check-in and how Gossil is intended to work beside Git. For application code, use the library examples and generated Rust API. The application manifest must select Gossil’s bundled libSQL provider as shown in those examples. The provider implements the Fossil date arithmetic required by artifact parsing and repository validation.

title: Get started
text: Choose a destination that does not exist: just gossil vcs init --admin-user alice example.gossil The receipt gives the project and server identifiers and the initial administrator password. Save the password privately. This command creates the empty root without a checkout or tracked files. It reads no preference file. See the initialization reference for date, hash and login options. An already installed mini-VCS preview has a separate command contract; these commands build the current source.

title: Get started
text: After the initialization above, create a directory and register it from source: mkdir example-work just gossil vcs open --repository example.gossil --checkout work --root example-work Open registers the initial empty root and writes a local lookup file, example-work/.gossil/checkout.json. Commands use that file to find and verify the checkout. It selects no files and requires no issue, project or author initialization. Configuration, permissions and existing markers can refuse the operation. Read native checkout open before retrying a failure, because database commit and locator publication have distinct outcomes.

title: Get started
text: Use add and status to enroll exact file paths. Add stores tracking metadata without changing working files or storing file content. Status lists every tracked path with its pending or recorded state and actual scope. New paths have unselected scope. The scope and commit commands select immutable scopes and record the complete private tracked tree. The development guide records the qualification boundary between source, release and installation.

Start in the Gossil source repository root after setup. This example runs gos through Cargo and keeps its database outside the working root. title: Bounded Fossil glob port
text: The glob module ports list parsing, matching and SQL expression construction from Fossil src/glob.c. It calls sqlite3_strglob from the selected libSQL 0.10.0 engine. The direct libsql-ffi dependency requests that exact version with default features disabled. The existing Cargo patch selects the accepted vendored provider for this dependency too. glob_create stores reusable patterns. Its glob_match method returns the first matching pattern’s one-based index, or zero. glob_multi_match scans once, using Fossil’s 100-byte temporary pattern buffer and allocating for longer patterns. Rust owns the buffers instead of calling glob_free. The list grammar uses commas and ASCII whitespace (bytes 9 through 13 and space). Single and double quotes retain commas and whitespace in a pattern. An unmatched opening quote consumes the rest of the list. Only a quote at the start of a term opens quoted parsing. There is no escape syntax. Empty quoted terms remain real empty patterns; absent, empty and delimiter-only lists have no patterns. Lists, candidates and SQL value expressions end at the first NUL byte, as in C. glob_expr produces SQL bytes and doubles apostrophes in patterns. The value argument must be a trusted SQL expression. The function does not quote or sanitize that argument. Use a trusted column expression or parameter expression such as ?1; bind an untrusted candidate separately through a caller-owned SQL interface. The function returns bytes and executes no SQL. After a closing quote, SQL construction skips one more byte, as the source does. For example, 'a'bc gives matching patterns a and bc, but SQL terms a and c. Do not normalize this distinction. SQL output joins terms with OR inside parentheses; a list with no patterns returns 0. A quoted empty pattern produces a real GLOB '' term. Callers supply finite Limits for list bytes, candidate bytes, pattern count and expression bytes; reusable matching retains its candidate limit. Byte limits apply to the prefix before the first NUL. Finding that prefix scans until the first NUL or the end of the original slice. Reservations are fallible and capacity additions are checked. Typed errors retain allocation failures. The one-shot matcher returns as soon as a pattern matches; it need not inspect later terms against the pattern-count budget. SQLite owns wildcard syntax, Unicode character handling and matching recursion. These byte budgets bound accepted prefixes and allocations; they do not bound SQLite matching CPU time or stack use. SQL execution can impose further engine limits on patterns and expressions. Matching follows SQLite GLOB rules. It is case sensitive, * can cross / and match dot-prefixed names, and backslashes are literal bytes rather than escapes. Character classes include ranges such as [a-c] and negation such as [^a]. The selected-engine controls include ? matching é, invalid UTF-8 bytes and an unmatched [ that matches nothing. Both gossil and gos accept vcs or its alias v. gossil vcs test-glob PATTERN STRING ... prints the SQL expression, parsed patterns and the indices returned by glob_match and glob_multi_match. The adapter uses fixed finite budgets of 1 MiB per list or candidate, 65,536 patterns and 16 MiB per expression. It rejects setting names beginning with @; repository settings remain a follow-up. JSON rendering also remains a follow-up. Unix arguments retain their exact bytes. On other platforms, the adapter accepts Unicode arguments as UTF-8 and rejects arguments that cannot be represented as Unicode. It does not replace invalid characters. The historical qualification used Unix targets only. Non-Unix conversion has source review, without cross-compilation or runtime qualification.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: The gossil::history module finds paths and common ancestors in caller-supplied check-in rows. Use it to inspect graph behavior in memory with finite input and search limits. Its algorithms come from Fossil’s path.c and pqueue.c. On this page, “native” means those algorithms and their queue order. The caller supplies the graph and resolves its branch and time metadata. This module opens no database and grants no permission to read repository history. The broader history API remains partial. Persistence, branch management and sync remain separate work.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Graph::new borrows a slice of Checkin metadata and indexes the supplied links. Each check-in needs a unique positive rid, branch bytes without NUL and a finite Julian-day time. A Julian day is the numeric count of days that Fossil uses for time. The caller resolves native branch defaults and missing times before construction. ParentLink supplies a parent, child and primary-parent flag for each plink row. Cherrypick supplies a source, destination and exclusion flag for each cherrypick row. Both endpoints must occur in the check-in slice. Keep the native query order of both slices of rows, with their duplicates and excluded cherrypicks. Construction keeps the row order of each direction, and it sorts only a separate index of identifiers. A new order of the rows can change which path of equal cost a search returns. The retained native capture script queries child and parent plink rows without ORDER BY. The field query_rows in the recorded fixture retains the observed order. This graph API imposes no database query order.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Call Result and purpose Graph::new(nodes, links, cherries, limits) Validate metadata and index ordered graph rows. graph.shortest(from, to, options) Return an owned Path between two known check-ins, or Ok(None) when the search finds no path. graph.common_ancestor(me, you) Return an Ancestor with a shared pivot and a diagnostic path, or Ok(None) when the search finds no ancestor. For shortest, set these Options explicitly: Option Behavior primary_only Skip non-primary parent links. direction: Direction::Both Search backwards until the first forward step, then forwards only. direction: Direction::Forward Search from parent to child only. direction: Direction::ForwardWithCherrypicks Also permit a non-excluded cherrypick as the first edge only. hidden Keep these known identifiers traversable and charge their cost, but exclude hidden steps from bisect counts. branch_cost: 0 Charge one per node, including the starting node. branch_cost: positive Start at zero, then charge absolute time distance plus this penalty for each branch change. The starting node remains visible even when its identifier occurs in hidden. A positive branch cost must fit i32. A search with a positive branch cost can return a path with more edges than the unweighted path, because it minimizes a different cost. The native queue does not take equal costs in first-in, first-out (FIFO) order. On insertion, a heap parent with an equal cost stays in place. On removal, the queue swaps through equal costs and prefers the left child on a tie. A shortest-path search visits the child rows before the backwards rows. These rules and the order of the input rows decide each tie. common_ancestor searches backwards from both endpoints. If either endpoint is zero, it returns Ok(None). If the two endpoints are equal, known and positive, it returns a path of one element. The returned path can start at either requested endpoint, because the native order of discovery sets its orientation.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Path.steps includes both endpoints. Each Step contains its identifier, a from_is_parent direction flag and its hidden status. Path.cost contains the native cumulative cost. For a shortest path, from_is_parent is true when the preceding step is the parent of this step. The first step has no preceding edge. Ancestor paths keep the native rewiring behavior, which can leave a direction flag false. So the flags of an ancestor path do not say whether the preceding step is the parent. Path::visible_steps counts non-hidden elements after the starting element. midpoint counts backwards from the destination, and it returns no element when the path has fewer than two visible steps. search_depth estimates the number of bisect comparisons that remain as the ceiling of log2 of the visible count. It returns zero for a count below two. These helpers describe the returned path. They do not implement a persisted bisect session or authorize access to its elements.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: There is no default Limits value. Choose every bound for the application: Field Bound checkins Number of supplied check-ins; also limits the length of hidden. links Combined number of parent and cherrypick rows, including excluded rows. branch_bytes Sum of all supplied branch byte lengths. search_nodes Allocated search records, including duplicate pending records. row_visits Adjacency rows inspected by each search, including filtered rows. The bounds limit counts and traversal, and not the total bytes on the heap. Error::Limit reports exhausted bounds. InvalidGraph reports malformed metadata, unknown identifiers or a cyclic chain of predecessors inside a search. NonFiniteCost reports an overflow in a time difference or in the cumulative cost. Allocation keeps the typed error of the failed reservation. A failed search returns no partial path. When the search finds no path, it succeeds with None. Graph validation checks the shape of the supplied data. Derived plink rows alone cannot establish provenance, private membership or complete history. A future storage adapter needs its own checks of admission and scope before it supplies rows.

title: Gossil
text: Gossil aims to keep agent work, issues and file history together alongside Git. Fossil is a version-control system. This build exposes a Rust library for Fossil’s delta bytes, artifact parsing and local storage. The gossil command creates, applies and checks deltas between files without a version-control checkout. It also initializes an empty repository through vcs init, without creating a checkout. The source vcs open command registers or reopens one native checkout and publishes its lookup locator without selecting files. The CLI and library also select explicit path scopes and record a complete private tracked tree while the shared root stays empty. Scope assigns a tracked path to shared or owner-local private history. Shared recording remains planned. Start with a file round trip, browse the CLI reference, or use the Rust API reference. Use working with repositories to plan agent files alongside Git. It explains checkouts, stored history and the intended private and shared workflows. For an already installed development preview, try the disposable file-history walkthrough. The preview is unmerged. Read compare Gossil with Git for the planned coordination of file history, exact issue state and versioned links to code. The examples show library calls for deltas, compressed bytes, hashes and token escaping. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. The converters in the module table use its task, project and author record model. Use vcs info to show the current recorded checkout and its shared and private heads.
